newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's financial sector reform plan welcomed.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's financial sector reform plan welcomed.

text.p: Plans by Pakistan's new caretaker government to reform state-run banks and financial institutions drew a welcome from analysts in Karachi on Monday.
Bad debts held by such institutions rose to 113.2 billion rupees at the end of fiscal 1995/96 (July-June) from 101 billion rupees a year earlier, central bank figures show.
Analyst Nauman Sheikh of KASB & Co said restructuring the state-owned financial sector through faster privatisation or mergers should be taken as a positive signal.
Kalim Aziz, head of research at ING Baring Securities, said publicly-owned financial institutions were draining the exchequer and had been widely abused for lending for political purposes.
"Consolidation through merger would be the best way to cut the fat," he told Reuters, but said it could be hard to deal with the hundreds of employees of the loss-making concerns.
He said the World Bank, which had sunk millions of dollars in these organisations in the past, had been advising the ousted government of Benazir Bhutto to get rid of them.

The Finance Ministry, led by Shahid Javed Burki, who has taken leave of absence from his job as a World Bank vice president, said on Sunday it planned to restructure or merge certain state-owned financial institutions, not scrap them.

The statement was issued a day after Burki said at his first news conference that the government would "abolish, consolidate or reform" the Industrial Development Bank of Pakistan, Pakistan Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation (PICIC), Regional Development Finance Corporation and others insitutions.
His remarks caused confusion in the stock market, where financial analysts said they did not fully understand what the caretaker government led by Meraj Khalid had in mind.
Newspapers on Monday said panicky depositors had withdrawn an estimated total of 210 million rupees ($5.22 million) on Sunday in a virtual run on the institutions Burki had named.
"The institutions probably should not have been identified by name," said one foreign economist, who asked not to be named. "Now they (the government) are trying to contain the damage."
Aziz said the panic had not been necessary. "It must be a misunderstanding," he said, adding that institutions sitting on billions of rupees could not be liquidated overnight.
PICIC shares swung wildly on the Karachi Stock Exchange on Monday, jumping 1.75 rupees, or 35 percent, to touch 6.75 before falling back to 6.00 rupees at the close.
"Yesterday the stock price tumbled on news reports that the government planned to liquidate PICIC. Now there is news of its merger which has pushed its price up," dealer Sajjad Mankani said.
Sunday's statement from the Finance Ministry did not say specifically that PICIC, which is already 55.44 percent owned by the private sector, would be merged.

It said that government-owned corporations, such as State Life Insurance Corporation, which hold the rest of the equity, might be asked to give up their holdings in PICIC to make it more efficient and independent.
